Please improve this email "The long-term larger vision is for application owners to be able to define their applications in EmpowerID and manage their authorization assignments and policies using either a coarse-grained (app rights and app roles) or fine-grained (app rights, app roles, field values aka “context”) model. Customers wish to avoid calling back to a central PDP due to latency and single point of failure so the architecture will support a distributed “offline” PDP model which, if the spike is successful, would be fulfilled by OPA. Distributed OPA instances would “pull” down just the JSON data needed for the applications they serve as PDP. The OPA PDP should offer a variety of authorization calls/endpoint methods such as: 1) asking for all specific UI resources for which the user has any access assignment in that app, 2) passing a username, application, optionally a resource, and a right and retrieving all context/constraints/field type values the user has for that right cross their assignments. 3) passing a username, application, right, optional resource, and constraint values and returning a true/false authorization decision. 4) passing a username, application, database table name, and returning the constraints to be used/injected as where clause filters in the apps data access layer. 

These are just some of the scenarios we wish to support. For the initial spike, we want to use JSON data that is an approximation of the PBAC policy data in EmpowerID and create a rego file that we can test in a simple .NET app to validate this as a workable solution. After this is proven, we’ll move into the details of designing various best practice application templates or an SDK to leverage this new model and then the harder work of how we will support the data flow for this distributed OPA model where the data lives in a central SQL database but is shipped or pulled down to distributed OPA instances.

tions. Recent works have shown that chain-

els to solve complex reasoning tasks, step-by-

CoT methods is restricted to very large LMs
such as GPT-3 (175B), thus limiting deploy-
ability. In this paper, we revisit the fine-
tuning approach to enable complex reasoning
in smaller LMs, optimized to efficiently per-
form a specific task. We propose Fine-tune-
CoT, a method that leverages the capabilities

ples and teach smaller models via fine-tuning.

model sizes. We find that Fine-tune-CoT en-
ables substantial reasoning capability in small
models, whereas previous prompt-based base-
lines exhibit near-random performance. Stu-
dent models can even outperform the teacher
in some tasks while reducing model size re-
quirements by several orders of magnitude.
We conduct extensive ablations and sample

eral important nuances that have been over-

We're focusing a lot within search on finding specific people, and we're focusing a lot on mapping out all of the world's media and places for recommendations -- but we haven't focused much on people recommendations at all. Once the linker has completed the symbol resolution step, it has associated each symbol reference in the code with exactly one symbol definition (i.e., a symbol table entry in one of its input object modules). At this point, the linker knows the exact sizes of the code and data sections in its input object modules. It is now ready to begin the relocation step, where it merges the input modules and assigns run-time addresses to each symbol. Relocation consists of two steps:

Relocating sections and symbol definitions. In this step, the linker merges all sections of the same type into a new aggregate section of the same type. For example, the .data sections from the input modules are all merged into one section that will become the .data section for the output executable object file. The linker then assigns run-time memory addresses to the new aggregate sections, to each section defined by the input modules, and to each symbol defined by the input modules. When this step is complete, each instruction and global variable in the program has a unique run-time memory address.

Relocating symbol references within sections. In this step, the linker modifies every symbol reference in the bodies of the code and data sections so that they point to the correct run-time addresses. To perform this step, the linker relies on data structures in the relocatable object modules known as relocation entries, which we describe next.

One of the main challenges of traditional co-creation processes is the lack of an incentive structure for individual creators. Many platforms that enable co-creation do not provide a way for creators to share in the economic value of their contributions, which can lead to a lack of motivation and engagement. This can hinder the ability of co-creation processes to tap into the full potential of the collective knowledge, expertise, and creativity of participating individuals.
Another challenge of traditional co-creation processes is the concentration of value creation among large companies. In these processes, it is often the case that big companies accrue the majority of the value created, leaving little for individual creators. This can create a power imbalance and limit the participation and engagement of smaller players, who may not have the same resources and influence as larger companies.
A third challenge of traditional co-creation processes is the difficulty of tracing and assigning parentage to contributions. This can create frustration and discouragement among participants, as it is often unclear who is responsible for which contributions and how they will be compensated. Without a clear and fair system for attributing value to contributions, co-creation processes may not fully capture the potential value of the collective effort.

Please use the Socratic method to teach me ALL of the following lesson section. Do not ask more than one question at a time, and do not answer any question yourself:

Branches Are Pointers
While the focus of this lesson was more advanced tools for changing Git history, we’re going into another advanced topic that might be hard for some to understand - Pointers. You’ve already learned about branches in the Rock Paper Scissors revisited lesson and how these hold multiple alternate reality versions of our files. Now we’re going to discuss what that actually means under the hood, and what it means for branches to be pointers.

Before we dive into branches, let’s talk about commits. If you recall this Git basics lesson from foundations, they were described as Snapshots. If it helps, think of this in a very literal sense. Every time you type in git commit, your computer is taking a picture of all the file contents that have been staged with git add. In other words, your entire tracked workspace gets copied.

So what is a branch? Based off of your exposure, you might be visualizing a branch as a group of commits. This actually isn’t the case! A branch is actually a pointer to a single commit! Hearing this, your first thought might be “Well if a branch is just a finger pointing at a single commit, how does that single commit know about all the commits that came before it?” The answer to this question is very simple: Each commit is also a pointer that points to the commit that came before it! Wow. This might be a lot to take in, so let’s take a moment to absorb that fact.

Now that you’ve had a second to gather your thoughts and attempt to wrap your head around this concept, it might help to go back and look at a concrete example of pointers we used in this lesson. Let’s think back to our use of git rebase -i HEAD~2. If you can remember, this command lets us edit the last two commits. Do you have any guesses on how Git knew which two commits to edit? That’s right, by using pointers! We start at HEAD, which is a special pointer for keeping track of the branch you’re currently on. HEAD points to our most recent commit in the current branch. That commit points to the commit made directly before it, which we can call commit two. That’s how git rebase -i HEAD~2 starts with a HEAD pointer, and then follows subsequent pointers to find which two commits to edit.

You might be feeling overwhelmed at this point, so let’s recap what we’ve learned. A branch is simply a pointer to a single commit. A commit is a snapshot, and it’s a pointer to the commit directly behind it in history. That’s it!

 2. Poor security configuration - IoT devices are often not securely configured, which can expose them to attacks. For example, some devices have weak or guessable passwords.
 3. Poor firmware updates - IoT devices often have weak firmware update mechanisms, which can allow attackers to install malicious firmware on the device.
 4. Poor physical security - IoT devices are often not properly secured against physical attacks. For example, some devices have weak physical security, such as thin plastic cases, which can be easily opened by attackers.

You’ll need to make sure both hosts have a shared network that they can communicate over, and that you’ve properly configured them with a common IP network, DNS servers, etc. Then you can just use the Move-VM cmdlet:
 

 $host1 = Get-VMHost -Name “hostname1”
 $host2 = Get-VMHost -Name “hostname2”
 Move-VM -Name “VMName” -VM $host1 -VM $host2 -Confirm:$false -Path “NewStorageLocation”
 

 You can specify the path to the new storage location in the -Path parameter, and you can add the -Confirm:$false switch to skip the confirmation prompt when you run the script. Make sure you check the script carefully before you run it to make sure it does what you want.
 

 Note that this will only work with certain hypervisors, such as Hyper-V and VirtualBox. If you’re trying to move between different hypervisors, you’ll need to look into tools like nsx-t.

 f(x,y)=7e^(-7x-7y)

 f(x)=∫f(x,y)dy=7e^(-7x)

Alright, great! I’m happy to help you learn about the summons and complaint (S&C) and bill of particulars (BP) here. So, the S&C is the complaint that the plaintiff files with the court, and it must be signed by the plaintiff or an attorney for the plaintiff. The BP is the response that the defendant must file with the court.  
 

 The S&C must include the following:
 

 1. The defendant’s name and address.
 

 2. The relief demanded (e.g. money damages).
 

 3. A short and plain statement of the claim showing that the plaintiff is entitled to the relief demanded.
 

 4. The facts showing that the defendant is liable for the relief demanded.
 

 5. The amount of damages demanded.
 

 6. The signature of the plaintiff or plaintiff’s attorney.
 

 The BP must include the following:
 

 1. The relief demanded (e.g. money damages).
 

 2. A statement of the defendant’s defenses.
 

 3. The facts showing that the defendant is not liable for the relief demanded.
 

 4. The signature of the defendant.
 

 The S&C and BP must both be filed with the court, and the defendant must be given a specific amount of time to respond to the S&C and BP. Once the defendant has responded to the S&C and BP, the case is ready for trial.

Suppose a client sends a POST request to a RESTful HTTP endpoint to create a resource. Which header should the HTTP server include in the response, to indicate the location of the newly created resource?
 A. content
 B. Location
 C. Link
 D. Server

The correct answer here is “B. Location”. The Location header specifies the URL for the newly created resource, and is the standard way to indicate the location of a newly created resource in a RESTful system. The other options are not appropriate headers for this purpose.

 A. There's a limit to how many times per second POST requests can be cached by a browser.
 B. Unlike GET requests, POST method request are always idempotent.
 C. Post requests remain in the browser history only until the window is closed.
 D. There's a length limit of the data you send with GET requests.

The difference between these two methods is that a GET request returns a resource from the server, whereas a POST request creates a new resource on the server. There are other differences as well, such as that a GET request can be cached by the browser, whereas a POST request is never cacheable. The other differences you mention are not correct.

Say you work for a startup that has hit hockey stick growth. You need to horizontally scale the database to support the increased usage. What are the trade offs between replicating vs sharding your database?
 A. Replication maintains better consistency guarantees at the cost of partitioning tolerance.
 B. Sharding makes partition tolerance hard but support better availability 
 C. Replication is easy, but does not bring all the benefit of complete shardin, if you can fully shared, you should.
 D. Sharding enable increased storage capacity and higher load.

There are two main tradeoffs here. First, replication provides stronger consistency guarantees but is less tolerant to network partitions, while sharding provides better partition tolerance but with weaker consistency. Second, replication is much easier to implement than sharding, so if you can get away with using replication you may prefer to do so. However, if you need to scale your system to handle a large amount of traffic, you will probably want to use sharding rather than replication. The other answers are not accurate characterizations of these tradeoffs.

Sure, a Data Lake is a centralized, scalable repository for storing all of an organization’s data in its native format, which could be structured, semi-structured, or unstructured. A Data Warehouse is a data mart optimized for reporting and analytics, where data is summarized and optimized for query performance. The two are complementary and often work together, with the Data Lake serving as the source of data for the Data Warehouse. Some common examples of Data Lakes include Amazon S3, Azure blob storage, and Snowflake, while Data Warehouses are typically implemented as a relational database, such as Oracle or DB2.
Is snowflake a data lake?

Yes, Snowflake is a cloud-based Data Lake. It provides a unified data warehouse service that combines the scale, performance, and simplicity of a data lake with the query optimization and data security of a data warehouse. Snowflake stores data in its native format, with full support for structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data types, and enables easy integration with popular BI and data analytics tools. It also offers advanced security features, such as data-level encryption, role-based access controls, and data lineage tracking.

When a bean is autowired, the framework examines the properties and methods of the bean, and based on their types, it will attempt to find a matching bean that can be injected as a dependency. Give detailed table wise examples of primary key, composite primary key and foreign key in database

Here are some table-wise examples of primary keys, composite primary keys, and foreign keys in databases:
 

 Primary key:
 

 -  Unique, non-null value
 -  Usually a single column
 -  Primary key value must not be a duplicate
 

 Composite primary key:
 

 -  Multiple columns combined to create a unique value
 -  Each column in the composite primary key must not be a duplicate
 -  Must not contain any NULL values
 

 Foreign key:
 

 -  Column(s) in one table that link(s) to the primary key of another table
 -  Foreign key(s) may contain NULL values
 -  Foreign key(s) must not be a duplicate

Talk to me about microservices patterns

Sure! Microservices are an architectural pattern for building software systems that are composed of small independent services. Each service runs in its own process and communicates with other services using well-defined interfaces, typically over a network. Microservices are usually developed and deployed independently, and can be updated and scaled without affecting the other services. This makes them ideal for building large-scale distributed systems that are highly available and scalable, and easy to maintain and evolve. Some common microservices patterns include Service-to-Service Communication, Service Discovery, Circuit Breakers, and Event-Driven Architecture.
Talk about Service Registry, Load Balancer and Event Sourcing too

OK, here goes! A Service Registry is a database of services, which is used by other services to discover and communicate with the available services. A Load Balancer is a component that routes requests from clients to the appropriate services, based on some load balancing algorithm. Event Sourcing is a design pattern in which the state of a service is stored as a sequence of events, rather than as a set of persistent data. This makes it easier to reconstruct the state of the service from the events, which is useful for reproducing past states of the service and making it more resilient to failure. Finally, a common microservice pattern is Event-Driven Architecture, in which services communicate with each other using events rather than direct requests. This makes the system more scalable and resilient, since services do not need to be online all the time.

Billing automation is the use of software to automatically create, manage, and reconcile customer invoices. It can help businesses save time and money, reduce billing errors, and improve customer service. Common features of billing automation software include subscription management, recurring billing, invoice reconciliation, and payment processing.
What is subscription management

Subscription management is the process of managing customer subscriptions, including billing, renewals, cancellations, and upgrades. Subscription management software can help businesses automate these processes, saving time and reducing errors. Common features of subscription management software include recurring billing, automatic renewals, one-click upgrades, and self-service cancellation.
What is Work 365

Work 365 is a cloud-based billing and subscription management solution for Microsoft CSPs. It provides automated billing and subscription management for CSPs, helping them to streamline operations, improve customer service, and increase revenue. Work 365 includes features such as automated subscription renewals, streamlined customer management, revenue recognition, and comprehensive reporting.
What is a Microsoft CSP

A Microsoft CSP (Cloud Solution Provider) is a company authorized by Microsoft to sell and manage cloud-based solutions, including Office 365, Azure, and Dynamics 365. CSPs help customers deploy and manage these solutions, providing consulting, implementation, and support services. CSPs can also offer customized solutions built on Microsoft technology, such as billing automation, subscription management, and revenue recognition.
What is revenue recognition

Revenue recognition is the process of recognizing revenue for a company’s products or services. Revenue recognition software can help businesses automatically recognize revenue for recurring subscriptions, one-time fees, and product sales. Common features of revenue recognition software include automated subscription billing, revenue leakage detection, and invoice reconciliation.
What is invoice reconciliation

Invoice reconciliation is the process of matching customer invoices with corresponding transactions in a company’s accounting system. Invoice reconciliation software can help businesses automate this process, saving time and reducing errors. Common features of invoice reconciliation software include automated transaction matching, invoice batch processing, and multi-currency support.
What is an Indirect Microsoft Provider

Indirect providers can help customers deploy and manage Microsoft solutions, including Office 365, Azure, and Dynamics 365. What is a prototype chain?

In JavaScript, a prototype chain is an inheritance mechanism in which objects can be copied and modified from an original source object, and later modified again themselves, to create a new object. It can be thought of as a linked list of sorts, where each object has a “prototype” property pointing to a parent object. Objects in a prototype chain are called “prototypes”, and the first object in the chain is called the “root”. Call, apply, and bind are three related methods that allow you to manipulate prototypes. The JSON data format is often used for this purpose.
what is call, apply and bind

The “call” method takes a function as an argument, and returns a new function which will call the original function with a given set of arguments. The “apply” method takes two arguments, a function and an array of arguments, and returns a new function which will call the original function with the given arguments. The “bind” method takes a function and some arguments, and returns a new function which will call the original function with the given arguments. These three methods are often used to create wrapper functions that will call another function with a given set of arguments.

What is Distributed Computing
Distributed computing is a field of computer science that studies distributed systems, and develops new algorithms and protocols for distributed computing.
What are Distributed Systems

Distributed systems are computing systems that consist of multiple interconnected nodes that communicate with each other and perform computations cooperatively. These systems are used for a variety of applications including parallel processing, high-performance computing, cluster computing, cloud computing, grid computing, and large-scale data processing.
Difference between Parallel computing and Distributed computing

Parallel computing and distributed computing are related, but distinct, concepts in computer science. Parallel computing refers to the use of multiple processors or processing cores to perform computations in parallel. Distributed computing refers to the use of multiple interconnected computing nodes (e.g. servers) to perform computations cooperatively. Both parallel computing and distributed computing are used for large-scale data processing and high-performance computing, but they are distinct concepts with different characteristics and uses.
Characteristics of Distributed computing

Distributed computing systems have several characteristic features, including:
 

 - Scalability: Distributed computing systems can scale up or down easily, allowing them to handle large amounts of data and computation.
 

 - Fault tolerance: Distributed computing systems are often designed to be fault-tolerant, meaning that they can continue to operate in the presence of component failures.
 

 - Independence: Distributed computing systems are often designed to be independent of specific hardware or software platforms, allowing them to be deployed on a variety of computing environments.
 

 - Efficiency: Distributed computing systems can be highly efficient, allowing them to perform large-scale data processing and high-performance computing tasks quickly and reliably.

Here is the solution to this problem using Lagrange multipliers:
 

 

 The distance between the point (x,y) on the line x=y and the circle of radius 1 centered at (5,2) is given by:
 

 

 d(x,y) = (x-5)^2 + (y-2)^2 - 1
 

 We seek to minimize this distance with respect to x and y. To do this, we introduce Lagrange multipliers lambda and mu and write the resulting Lagrange function:
 

 

 L(x,y,lambda,mu) = (x-5)^2 + (y-2)^2 - 1 + lambda(x-y) + mu(x+y-7)
 

 We set the partial derivatives of L with respect to x and y equal to zero and solve for x and y:
 

 

 x = 5 + lambda/2
 

 y = 2 + lambda/2 - mu
 

 Plugging these solutions back into the equation for d(x,y), we get the minimum value:
 

 

 d(x,y) = (lambda/2)^2 + (lambda/2 - mu)^2 - 1
 

 For the second part of the problem, we consider what happens to this minimum distance if the circle is moved slightly away from the line x=y. Specifically, we assume that the center of the circle is moved from (5,2) to (5+e,2-e). We can approximate the resulting change in the minimum distance by expanding d(x,y) around e=0:
 

 

 d(x,y) = (lambda/2)^2 + (lambda/2 - mu)^2 - 1
 

 = (lambda/2)^2 + (lambda/2 - mu)^2 - 1 + 2e(lambda/2) - e^2(lambda/2 - mu)
 

 Assuming that e is small, we can approximate d(x,y) as:
 

 

 d(x,y) = (lambda/2)^2 + (lambda/2 - mu)^2 - 1 + 2e(lambda/2) - e^2(lambda/2 - mu)
 

 = (lambda/2)^2 + (lambda/2 - mu)^2 - 1 - e^2(lambda/2 - mu)
 

 The first two terms on the right-hand side are the minimum value of d(x,y) for the original circle centered at (5,2), and the last term is the approximate change in the minimum value due to the displacement of the circle. Thus, the approximate change in the minimum value is:
 

 

 -e^2(lambda/2 - mu)

what is the difference between data structure and ADT?

Data structures and abstract data types (ADTs) are related but distinct concepts in computer programming. Data structures are the actual physical representation of data in a computer program, while ADTs define abstract operations on the data that are not tied to a specific implementation. Some common examples of ADTs include lists, queues, and trees, while specific examples of data structures include arrays and linked lists.

What is a bad block? Describe the techniques to manage disk bad blocks. Or Describe 
 the methods to handle bad block?

A bad block is a region of a hard disk that has been damaged and is no longer readable by the disk controller. Common causes of bad blocks include physical damage to the disk surface, deterioration of the recording medium due to age, and magnetic interference from nearby magnetic fields. Techniques to manage disk bad blocks generally involve periodically scanning the disk surface for bad blocks and marking them as unusable, so that the disk controller can avoid reading them. Other methods involve transforming I/O requests into hardware operations that are robust to bad blocks, such as reading data from multiple locations and averaging the results.

Explain the steps of transforming an I/O request to hardware operations. Or What are the 
 steps involved in transforming an I/O request to hardware operations.

The steps of transforming an I/O request to hardware operations generally involve converting the request into a set of physical I/O operations. This typically involves determining the disk sector to be read or written, calculating the corresponding physical disk address, and sending the request to the disk controller. The disk controller then performs the requested I/O operation by reading data from or writing data to the corresponding disk sector.

Explain the different space allocation methods for storing files on disks and the type of 
 file access they support.

There are two main space allocation methods for storing files on disks: contiguous and non-contiguous. Contiguous space allocation stores files as a single contiguous block on the disk, while non-contiguous space allocation stores files as multiple blocks scattered across the disk. Contiguous space allocation is generally faster and more efficient for random file accesses, while non-contiguous space allocation is generally faster and more efficient for sequential file accesses.

A cult is generally defined as a religion or religious group that is considered to be unorthodox, new, or unfamiliar. The term often has a negative connotation, and cults are sometimes associated with controversial or suspicious activities.
List things that defines a cult

A cult generally has the following characteristics:
 

 1. It is relatively new or unfamiliar.
 

 2. It has a charismatic or authoritarian leader.
 

 3. It teaches doctrines that are unorthodox or non-traditional.
 

 4. It is relatively small and/or isolated.
 

 5. It often requires unquestioning devotion from its members.
What are examples of cults?

Some examples of cults include:
 

 1. The Church of Scientology.
 

 2. The Branch Davidians.
 

 3. The Heaven's Gate cult.
 

 4. The MOVE cult.
 

 5. The polygamous Mormon sect known as the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.
What are common patterns of the recruitment process of a cult?

The recruitment process of a cult typically involves the following steps:
 

 1. Persuasion: The recruiter uses various psychological techniques to convince potential recruits that joining the cult will bring them benefits.
 

 2. Information control: The recruiter limits the recruit's exposure to outside information, in order to prevent them from learning about the cult's controversial or negative aspects.
 

 3. Social isolation: The recruiter isolates the recruit from their family and friends, in order to make them more dependent on the cult.
 

 4. Emotional manipulation: The recruiter uses emotional manipulation techniques to control the recruit's emotions and thoughts.
 

 5. Brainwashing: The recruiter subjects the recruit to intense psychological pressure, in order to break down their critical thinking and instill obedience to the cult leader.
How to define a cult from a psychological perspective?

A cult can be defined psychologically as a group that uses psychological manipulation techniques to control the thoughts and behaviors of its members. The goal of this psychological manipulation is to induce obedience to the group leader and to promote the interests of the group. Cults typically require members to dedicate significant time and energy to the group, and often isolate members from their families and friends. They also typically promote a highly idealistic and optimistic view of the world, and use emotional manipulation techniques to control members' thoughts and behaviors.

what is expected value of a random variable

The expected value of a random variable is the average of its possible values. It is given by the following formula:
 

 E(X) = Σ(x*P(x))
 

 where X is the random variable, E(X) is the expected value, Σ is the sum, x ranges over all possible values of X, and P(x) is the probability of the event x occurring.

 E(X) = Σ(x*P(x)) = P(X=x1)*x1 + P(X=x2)*x2 + ...
why there is a need to multiply probability of an event

The expected value of a random variable X is the sum of the products of the probabilities of the different possible values of X and the value of X itself. This is because the expected value quantifies the expected outcome of a large number of trials of the random variable, and the probability of each possible outcome times the value of that outcome gives the contribution to the expected value.

what is virtual memory, Address space, memory space

The virtual memory of a computer system refers to a method of organizing and addressing the physical memory of a computer in an abstract way, so that the virtual memory can be referenced in a simpler, more intuitive way. The virtual memory is essentially a kind of “mapping” of the physical memory of the computer into a “logical” memory space that can be referenced in a simpler, more intuitive way. Address space refers to the space of addresses used to reference the memory of a computer. Memory space refers to the space of memory addresses used to reference the memory of a computer.
Address Mapping Using Pages: pages & blocks, page frame

The physical memory of a computer is broken down into pages and blocks, so that each page of memory is associated with a specific address within the address space. The physical memory pages are then grouped into larger units called page frames, which are managed by the operating system. The pages within a page frame are referred to as “virtual pages”, and can be referenced in the virtual memory space using simple, intuitive addresses.
Assocative memory page table

The address space is stored in a table called the “page table”, which is an associative array that maps virtual page addresses to physical page addresses. The page table is used by the processor to translate virtual memory addresses into physical memory addresses, and thus allow access to the physical memory of the computer. The page table is stored in the computer’s memory, and is updated by the operating system in response to various events, such as process creation, memory allocation, and page faults.

Define the following terms in brief, along with examples:
 - Virtual Machine
 - Host and Guest Operating system
 - Abstraction
 - Server Sprawl

- Virtual Machine: A software-based computing environment that acts as an independent computer system, running its own operating system and applications. Virtual machines are used for creating and running multiple “virtual” computers within a single physical machine.
 - Host and Guest Operating Systems: A host operating system is the main operating system running on a physical machine, while a guest operating system is a virtual machine running within the host OS. The host OS provides the resources (CPU, memory, storage, network) for the guest OS to run on.
 - Abstraction: A simplified or idealized representation of something abstract or concrete. Abstraction is essential for creating virtual machines, as it allows the host OS to abstract away all the specifics of the underlying physical hardware, so that the guest OS thinks it is running on a regular computer.
 - Server Sprawl: A situation where multiple virtual machines are running on a single physical machine, consuming significant resources and causing inefficient utilization of hardware. Server sprawl is a major concern in cloud computing environments.

 1. Fork the gitlab repository to your own account.

 3. Clones the forked gitlab repository.
 4. Finds and downloads the config.json and other custom assets from a configured location.

Sure, here is an example of steps 3 to 6:
 

 3. Create a new directory in the ansible playbook:

  cp /configs/config.json /tmp/playbooks/gitlab/
  cp /configs/custom_assets/* /tmp/playbooks/gitlab/

  - name: Install gitlab
  become: yes
  apt:
  name: gitlab
  state: present
 

  - name: Clone the gitlab repository

Treatment for these problems usually involves speech therapy, which can help the baby learn to make sounds more effectively.
What are some common vocal cord problems in babies?

The most common vocal cord problems in babies are laryngitis and laryngomalacia. Laryngitis is inflammation of the vocal cords, which can make it difficult for the baby to make sounds. Laryngomalacia is a softening or weakness of the vocal cords, which can cause the baby to make a stridor sound when breathing. Both of these conditions are usually treatable with speech therapy.
What is a stridor sound?

A stridor sound is a high-pitched squeaking sound that occurs when breathing. It is caused by weakness or softening of the vocal cords, and is often heard in babies with laryngomalacia. Stridor is usually not a cause for concern, and will often resolve on its own with time. However, if it persists or gets worse, it may indicate a more serious problem, such as laryngitis.

what is a rank of matrix in simple words?

The rank of a matrix is the smallest number of linear independent rows (or columns) that can be used to represent the matrix. A matrix with rank n can be represented using n linear independent rows (or columns), and any matrix with more than n linear independent rows (or columns) is said to be “non-singular”.
what is singular vs non-singular matrix?

A singular matrix has at least one linear independent row or column, and therefore has rank less than or equal to the number of rows or columns. A non-singular matrix has no linear independent rows or columns, and is therefore said to be “full rank”. A non-singular matrix can always be transformed into row echelon form by a sequence of column operations, and also has a unique inverse.
what is row echlon form

Row echelon form is a special form of a matrix that can always be obtained by applying a sequence of column operations to a non-singular matrix. In row echelon form, the leading diagonal entries are non-zero, and the sub-diagonal entries are all zero. Row echelon form is useful because it allows for quick computation of the determinant and inverse of a matrix.

In this example, several transcription errors could occur, including:
 

 1) Phonetic errors - This type of error results from the transcription program not being able to correctly recognize the speech patterns in the sentence. For example, if the speaker pronounced the word "doing" with a long "o" sound, the transcribed text might read "doin'."
 

 2) Omissions - This type of error occurs when the speech-to-text program fails to transcribe an entire word or phrase. For example, if the speaker paused briefly before saying "today," the transcribed text might read "how are you doing today."
 

 3) Insertions - This type of error occurs when the speech-to-text program transcribes an extra word or phrase that was not actually spoken. For example, if the speaker pronounced the word "doing" with a short "o" sound, the transcribed text might read "Hi, how are you doing today?"
 

 4) Word-level errors - This type of error occurs when the speech-to-text program transcribes a word incorrectly. For example, if the speaker pronounced the word "doing" with a long "o" sound, the transcribed text might read "Hi, how are you doing today?"

What is biometric system

Biometric system is an identification system that uses biological characteristics to distinguish one person from another. Biometric systems have a number of advantages over traditional systems of personal identification, such as passwords and pins. They are more secure, since they cannot be easily stolen or forgotten, and are more convenient, since they eliminate the need to remember or carry around a physical token. Biometric systems are also more accurate, since they are linked to a person’s unique biological characteristics.
Types of biometric system

There are two main types of biometric system: physical and behavioral. Physical biometric systems use physical characteristics such as fingerprints, facial geometry, or retinal patterns to identify a person. Behavioral biometric systems, on the other hand, analyze human behavioral characteristics such as speech patterns, walking style, or signature dynamics.
Defines user biometric system

A user biometric system is a system that uses biological characteristics of a user to distinguish that user from others. User biometric systems are typically used for security purposes, such as for logging into a computer, or for financial transactions.

In order to calculate cash flow, you’ll need to understand a few terms. The key financial statements are the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. The income statement shows how much money a company made or lost in a given period, the balance sheet shows what the company owns and owes at a particular point in time, and the cash flow statement shows how much cash came into and went out of the company during a given period. Cash flow is calculated by taking the changes in cash and cash equivalents from the cash flow statement, and adding to that the cash provided by or used in operating, investing, and financing activities. Some of these activities are added to the cash flow, and some are subtracted, so you’ll need to understand which is which.
explain in more detail which ones are added/subtracted

The cash provided by operating activities is added to cash flow, as this represents cash coming into the company from its normal business operations. The cash used in operating activities is subtracted, as this represents cash going out of the company from its normal business operations. The cash provided by (or used in) investing activities is added (or subtracted), as this represents cash coming into (or going out of) the company from investing activities, such as the purchase or sale of property, plant, and equipment. The cash provided by (or used in) financing activities is added (or subtracted), as this represents cash coming into (or going out of) the company from financing activities, such as the issuance or repayment of debt or equity.
give formula for cfo

why

Cash flow from operations is a measure of the amount of cash generated by a company’s normal business operations during a given period. It represents the cash generated by the company’s day-to-day operations, which can be used for paying expenses, investing in new projects, or returning to shareholders. The formula for cash flow from operations is simply the difference between cash provided by operating activities and cash used in operating activities.

A legacy system is an outdated computer system that no longer meets the needs of the organization. They are also often prone to security vulnerabilities.

 • Legacy web servers
 

 • Legacy operating systems
 

 • Legacy applications

What does no longer supported by their vendor mean?

That means that the vendor of the software no longer provides updates, patches, or other support for the software. This can be a significant problem, because if the software has known security vulnerabilities, the organization is vulnerable to attack. And if the software doesn’t have the features the organization needs, they are essentially stuck with a system that doesn’t meet their needs.

What is PCA?

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a type of dimensionality reduction that is commonly used in data analysis. It allows you to take a set of high-dimensional data and to reduce it down to a lower-dimensional representation that still preserves the important information in the data.
How does the reduction really happens in PCA?

PCA works by performing an eigen-value decomposition on the covariances or correlation matrix of your data. This allows you to express your data in terms of a set of “eigen-values” and “eigen-vectors”, which are the principal components. The dimensionality of your data is then reduced by keeping only the leading (most significant) eigen-vectors, which capture the majority of the variation in the data.
What is mean by eigen value decomposition and covarince matrix?

Eigenvalue decomposition is a mathematical procedure for finding a set of “eigenvalues” and “eigenvectors” for a given matrix. The eigenvalues are the “principal components” that are associated with the matrix, and the eigenvectors are the corresponding “principal directions” in the data space. Thecovariance matrix is simply a matrix that contains the covariances of the variables in your data set. PCA performs an eigen-value decomposition on this covarianc matrix in order to find the principal components.
difference between covarience, corealation and variance and standard deviation along with formula and Distributive laws

The main difference between covariances and correlations is that covariances measure the linear association between two variables, whereas correlations also take into account the magnitude of the association. Variance is a measure of the “scatter” or “variation” in a data set, and standard deviation is the square root of the variance. There are several distributive laws that are commonly used in statistics, including the distributive law of covariance and the distributive law of correlation. These allow you to express covariances and correlations in terms of the individual variable covariances and correlations.
what is unit vectors?

Unit vectors are simply vectors with length 1. They are used in linear algebra to express directions in a vector space. For example, you can use unit vectors to express the “x-axis” and “y-axis” directions in a 2-dimensional coordinate system. Unit vectors are also useful in PCA, because they allow you to express your data in terms of principal directions in the data space.

Explain domain driven design. Compare it with Set driven design. Give example for Todo application.

Domain Driven Design (DDD) is a set of principles and practices for modeling and developing software systems that are strongly tied to a specific domain. It emphasizes the use of a core domain model, which is developed iteratively in conjunction with the domain experts, in order to capture the underlying structure of the domain and support robust, maintainable, and scalable software.
 

 In contrast, Set Driven Design (SDD) emphasizes the use of a set of constraints to drive the design and implementation of a software system. In SDD, the constraints may be technical (e.g. specific programming languages or frameworks), or domain-specific (e.g. requirements derived from business goals), or a combination of both. In DDD, the core domain model is the driving force behind the design, while in SDD the constraints imposed by the chosen technologies or domain requirements play a more central role.
 

 In terms of a practical example, consider a simple Todo application. In DDD, we would model the core domain concepts (e.g. tasks, projects, users) as classes in a Domain Model, and develop the application around this model, allowing the model to drive the design of the application’s functionality. In SDD, we would instead focus on the technical constraints imposed by the chosen technologies (e.g. using a relational database for storage) or domain requirements (e.g. enforcing strict separation of user tasks into projects), and design the application around these constraints. The resulting application would be tightly coupled to the specific technologies and/or domain requirements chosen, and would be difficult to adapt to other contexts.

How good is QAGS metric to compare an AI generated summary output with ground truth summary? Explain with example. Tell strengths and weakness and caution areas.

QAGS (Quantitative Assessment of Generated Summaries) is a widely-used evaluation metric for automatically generated summaries. It is useful for comparing summaries produced by different systems, or summaries produced by the same system under different conditions.  
 

 The primary strength of QAGS is that it provides a relatively objective and quantitative assessment of summary quality. The primary weakness is that it only measures summary accuracy, and not other aspects of summary quality such as readability or clarity.  
 

 A related issue is that QAGS only provides a single overall score for a summary, rather than breaking down the score into component parts. Thus it is not as informative as some other evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE (Recall-Oriented UnderlyingGround-Truth Evaluation).  
 

 A final weakness of QAGS is that it is sensitive to small differences in summary quality, and may not be appropriate for comparing summaries produced by very different systems.  
 

 Overall, QAGS is a useful tool for comparing summaries produced by the same system under different conditions, or for comparing summaries produced by different systems, but it should be used with caution, and supplemented with other evaluation metrics where possible.
 

 Let’s take an example: Suppose you have two summaries of the same news article, one generated by a human and one generated by a machine. You can compare the machine generated summary with the human generated summary using QAGS. The human generated summary will probably get a higher score than the machine generated summary, because human generated summaries tend to be more accurate and comprehensive. However, the QAGS score will only measure summary accuracy, and not other aspects of summary quality such as readability or clarity.  
 

 In this case, you may also want to compare the machine generated summary with the original news article, to see how well the summary captures the main ideas of the article. You can use QAGS to compare the machine generated summary with the original article, but again you will only be measuring summary accuracy, and not other aspects of summary quality.

While computers can process large quantities of text and generate text in response, their understanding is generally very shallow and limited. In contrast, humans are capable of understanding language in a much deeper and more nuanced way, including recognizing the meaning of individual words, recognizing the relationship between words, and inferring the overall meaning of a text. If we use faiss for semantic search, there are two problems: Elastic Beanstalk has an autoscaling feature and can use multiple instances. However, writing to faiss doesn't work with concurrent processes. Thus, it is necessary to somehow synchronize the writing to faiss. The second problem is the loading time if the faiss index is located on a S3 bucket. The best way would be to hold faiss in memory, but then the difficulty is to keep this in memory index up to date.
 

 How should we solve these problems?

A solution for the first problem is to use some sort of database or in-memory cache to keep the faiss index synchronized across multiple instances. A simple way to do this would be to use a database like DynamoDB, or an in-memory cache like ElastiCache. The second problem can be solved by holding the faiss index in memory on each individual instance, and periodically flushing the index to a S3 bucket for backup. You can use a background worker process or cron job to perform these operations.
Would AWS SQS help somehow?

AWS SQS is a message queueing system that can be used to facilitate communication between different parts of an application. It could potentially be used to help with the first problem, by using SQS to synchronize writing to the faiss index across multiple instances. However, it’s not the best solution for this problem, since it would add significant overhead to the writing operations. A better solution would be to use a database or in-memory cache, as I mentioned above.
Can I use ElastiCache together with Elastic Beanstalk?

Yes, you can use ElastiCache together with Elastic Beanstalk. You can create a cache cluster in the same region as your Elastic Beanstalk environment, and configure Elastic Beanstalk to use the cache cluster for its in-memory index. This will allow you to keep the index up-to-date across multiple instances, without adding any additional overhead to the writing operations.

Define a Cooperative Process in OS. What are the three criteria a critical section problem solution needs to satisfy?

A cooperative process in OS is a program that allows other programs to execute in an interleaved manner. Critical section problems are synchronization problems that occur when multiple processes need to access shared resources simultaneously. Solutions to critical section problems need to satisfy three criteria: mutual exclusion, progress, and starvation-freedom. Mutual exclusion ensures that at most one process can be in a critical section at any given time. Progress ensures that eventually some process will be able to enter a critical section. Starvation-freedom prevents a process from being continuously pre-empted from entering a critical section.

Write and explain the Readers-Writers problem solution. Or
 Explain Reader-Writers problem solution using Semaphores

The Readers-Writers problem is a synchronization problem that occurs when multiple readers or writers need to access shared resources simultaneously. The solution is based on the use of semaphores, which are synchronization primitives that allow processes to wait for and signal that a shared resource is available. The Readers-Writers problem solution uses two semaphores, one for readers and one for writers. Readers are allowed to acquire the reader semaphore and access the shared resource simultaneously, as long as no writers are waiting for the resource. Writers are allowed to acquire the writer semaphore and access the shared resource simultaneously, as long as no readers are waiting for the resource. This solution satisfies the three criteria for critical section problems: mutual exclusion, progress, and starvation-freedom.

 Authority: Knowledge gained through an accepted source. For example, an expert’s testimony in court or a doctor’s diagnosis.

Is there a particular aspect of cell-mediated immunity that you’re interested in? For example, you might want to know about:
 

 -  T-cell subsets

 -  And so on.
T-cell subsets

The main types of T-cells are CD4+ T-cells and CD8+ T-cells, both of which can be further subdivided into subsets based on the T-cell surface marker (or “receptor”) expressed on their surface. CD4+ T-cells can be subdivided into T-helper (Th) cells and T-regulatory (Treg) cells. CD8+ T-cells can be subdivided into T-cytotoxic (Tc) cells and T-suppressor (Ts) cells.
surface markers

Each of these T-cell types can be identified based on the surface markers (receptors) they express. CD4+ cells express the CD4 surface marker, CD8+ cells express the CD8 surface marker, Th cells express the CD4 surface marker, Tc cells express the CD8 surface marker, Ts cells express both the CD4 and CD8 surface markers, and Treg cells express neither the CD4 nor CD8 surface markers.
T dependent

In the T-dependent immune response, antigens are processed by antigen presenting cells (APCs) and then presented to CD4+ T-cells, which then differentiate into Th cells and produce lymphokines that activate B-cells, which differentiate into plasma cells that produce antibodies.
T independent antigen

In the T-independent immune response, antigens are presented directly to CD8+ T-cells, which then differentiate into Tc cells and produce lymphokines that activate macrophages, which then phagocytose and destroy the antigen.
recognition of antigens by T cells

T-cells recognize antigens through the T-cell receptor (TCR), which is a complex of molecules on the surface of the T-cell that is able to bind to the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of the antigen presenting cell. The TCR contains a recognition site that binds to the peptide presented by the MHC, and also contains signaling components that allow the T-cell to respond to the bound peptide by producing lymphokines.
MHC

The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is a collection of genes on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs) that encode proteins involved in the recognition and processing of antigens. The main types of MHC molecules are the class I and class II molecules, which are expressed on the surface of the APC.
role of MHC

The role of the MHC is to process and present antigens to T-cells so that the T-cells can recognize the antigens and respond by producing lymphokines. The MHC molecules are anchored in the membrane of the APC, and they are composed of a number of different proteins that work together to present the antigens to the T-cells.

By using deception, security teams can identify and respond to threats before they cause real damage to the organization’s valuable assets. The key benefit of deception-based cybersecurity is that it creates a high level of uncertainty for attackers, making it difficult for them to identify the real assets from the fake ones. This makes it more expensive and time-consuming for attackers to conduct reconnaissance and increases the likelihood of them making a mistake, which can lead to their identification and capture. Additionally, deception-based cybersecurity can be used to detect insider threats, as the system can detect and alert when a legitimate user is accessing fake data or assets that they should not be accessing. The implementation of deception-based cybersecurity requires careful planning and design, as it involves the creation of a network of fake assets and data that must be convincing enough to deceive attackers. Furthermore, the system must be constantly monitored and updated to ensure that it remains effective and does not create new vulnerabilities or false positives. Real-time application of deception-based cybersecurity includes the use of honeypots, which are computer systems that are intentionally left vulnerable to attract attackers. Once an attacker interacts with the honeypot, security teams can monitor and analyze the attacker’s behavior to understand their tactics and motives, which can inform future security measures. Another application is the use of decoy files and data that appear valuable to attackers but contain fake or misleading information. These decoys can be used to distract and misdirect attackers, delaying their progress and giving security teams time to respond. In conclusion, deception-based cybersecurity is a valuable addition to traditional security measures, offering a proactive and cost-effective approach to identifying and responding to threats. The multi-armed bandit problem is a classic problem in statistics and operations research, and it poses a dilemma: how should a decision-maker balance exploration (trying out different options) and exploitation (using what they’ve learned from previous choices)?
explain the dilemma?

In the classic multi-armed bandit problem, there are a number of slot machines, or “arms”, and the player is trying to choose which one to play in order to maximize their expected reward. If the player always chooses the same machine, they will eventually get the best possible reward from that machine, but they may be missing out on better rewards from other machines they haven’t tried. On the other hand, if the player tries out every machine, they may end up wasting time and money on machines that don’t give them the best rewards.
explain epsilon greedy algorithms, its benefits and disadvantages.

An epsilon-greedy algorithm is one that alternates between exploring (trying out different machines) and exploiting (playing the machine that seems best based on previous experience). The epsilon-greedy algorithm is an example of a “greedy” algorithm, because it tries to maximize reward at each step, but the epsilon term means that it will sometimes choose to explore rather than exploit. The epsilon-greedy algorithm has the benefit of being simple and easy to implement, but it may not always perform well, because it doesn’t account for how much information the player has gathered so far.
explain UCB1 (Upper Confidence Bound) and its benefits and disadvantages.

In a network, the maximum flow problem is to find a flow (a transfer of resource, like water or electricity) from one node (a source) to another node (a sink) that is as large as possible. The global minimum cut problem is to find the smallest set of edges (a cut) that, if removed, will decrease the flow from the source to the sink as much as possible. Both of these problems are NP-hard, meaning that they are computationally intractable for large-scale problems, but there are very fast approximate algorithms for them, based on the Ford-Fulkerson and Edmons Karps algorithms. Here is a very basic complexity analysis of these algorithms.
explain complexity analysis in above

The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm has an O(V*E) time complexity, where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges. The Edmons Karps algorithm has an O(V*E*k) time complexity, where k is the size of the maximum flow. In both cases, the algorithms are very efficient in practice, since V and E are typically much smaller than k.
explain ford-fulkerson algorithm and edmond karp algorithm in detail with graphs

The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm works by finding a path from the source to the sink, and then repeatedly increasing the flow along that path by one unit. This process is repeated until the maximum flow is found. The algorithm is implemented as a loop over all edges in the network, and each iteration is O(V) in time.  
 The Edmons Karps algorithm also works by finding a path from the source to the sink, but instead of increasing the flow along that path by one unit each time, the algorithm increases the flow by a factor of k, where k is the maximum flow that can be found. This process is repeated until the maximum flow is found, and each iteration is O(k*V) in time.

The sub-network can be chosen in a variety of ways, such as by randomly selecting some edges to be part of the sub-network, or by randomly selecting some vertices to be part of the sub-network, or by randomly selecting some flow paths to be part of the sub-network. This randomization process can significantly reduce the computational time required to find the maximum flow.  -  transactions are broadcast to the network and then included in a block
 -  transactions are irreversible once included in a block
 -  each transaction has a unique identifier (TxHash)
 -  the order of transactions in a block is not determined in advance, but rather chosen by the miners
 -  miners receive fees for including transactions in a block
 -  recipients of transactions can choose to accept or reject them
 -  rejected transactions are not included in a block
 -  there is a limit on the number of transactions that can be included in a block

what is swapping in memory management

Swapping is the process of moving a program out of primary memory (such as RAM) and into secondary memory (such as hard disk), to free up space in primary memory. It is a form of memory management, which is the process of organizing and controlling the use of memory in a computer system. The specific algorithm used to decide which programs to swap out and which to keep in memory is called a “swap algorithm”. The most common swap algorithms are “first-fit” and “best-fit”. “First-fit” simply swaps out the program that has been in memory the longest, while “best-fit” tries to find the program that will cause the least amount of disruption to the system when it is swapped out. Other less common swap algorithms include “least-recently-used” (which tries to keep recently used programs in memory) and “random” (which chooses programs for swapping out at random). There are also more sophisticated swap algorithms that try to optimize performance by taking into account factors such as how important a program is to the system, how much data it has in memory, and so forth.

what is demand paging, copy on write and trashing

When this happens, the system must allocate more memory from the hard disk, which is much slower than memory in RAM. This results in decreased performance. “Copy-on-write” refers to a situation where two programs are trying to modify the same piece of memory at the same time. This can cause both programs to produce corrupted data. “Trashing” refers to when one program tries to allocate so much memory that it fills up the entire system, which results in the system crashing.

how can you teach kids about decision making

Here is the tooling manifesto:

# Background

Terra has experienced a surge of interest from developers since the addition of CosmWasm in Columbus-4, but its hasty transitional pivot toward "Terra-as-a-Platform" threatens to magnify critical issues regarding security, dev experience, transparency, testability, etc.

**Terran One** is a company that engages in many initiatives, unified under one simple theme: **build to help build.** We research, test, and develop dev tools and use those tools to inspire developers with apps that showcase what is possible when devs are properly equipped

Whereas TFL has mostly been BD-focused and never had a strong developer culture, Terran One aims to become its developer-sympathetic counterpart. We'll bring the philosophy of thoughtful, strategic consideration combined with aggressive pragmatism and resourcefulness — and apply it in giving much needed attention to the great underserved community of builders on Terra.

# Standard Model (SMF)

[Standard Model - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model)

**Standard Model** ([ref](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model)) is a framework for Terra smart contracts that defines a set of standard conventions for contracts for simple integration with Terran One tooling.

SMF provides a predictable structure which allow contract writers to access things like enhanced debugging & testing, logging, composability, contract administration, automated generation of docs, SDKs, UIs, etc.  

## Problem

The main impediment for strong tooling for CosmWasm comes from its permissive lack of constraints on WebAssembly. As CosmWasm can potentially run any correct WASM binary created through whatever process, the tremendous degrees of freedom introduced make it impossible to create great tooling that can target generic contracts. 

Potential troubling consequences:

- lack of clear guidance for best practices = everybody tries their own thing, or more commonly, "remix" and introduce
    - storage / retrieval of data
    - contract composability
- build process must be considered during contract verification — an attacker can VERY easily inject code at the end that modifies code into malicious

## Intended Effect

- Establishes **Terran One** as a reputable authority among developers (currently a niche that's hard to target for many teams and even TFL itself)
- Create a systematized way of creating smart contracts with predictable structure. This way, we can focus on tooling (aggressive automation) that targets every dApp we build.
- Create an ecosystem of projects which follow the Standard Model.

and other invaders, through a series of steps called the immune response.

the sum of all naturally occurring defense mechanisms that protect
humans from diseases. The immune system, which is made up of special
cells, proteins, tissues, and organs, defends people against invaders
, keeping people healthy and preventing infections.
There are two types of resistance
1-Non-specific (innate)
2-Specific (acquired)
Non-specific immunity, as the name suggests, is not specific to a certain
group of micro-organisms. These defense mechanisms act against each
and every invader of the body.
Anatomical barriers include physical, chemical and biological barriers.
Skin is the first barrier and the first mechanism of non-specific defense.
The epithelial surfaces form a physical barrier that is impermeable to
most infectious agents, acting as the first line of defense against invading
organisms.
Desquamation of skin epithelium also helps remove bacteria and other
infectious agents that have adhered to the epithelial surfaces. presence of
sebaceous glands in the dermis provides an environment unsuitable for
the survival of microbes. presence of sweat glands that secrete sweat
which washes infections off(High salt content of sweat dries microorganisms off)
The flushing action of tears and saliva helps prevent infection of the
eyes and mouth. Saliva contains anti-bacterial properties due to
lysozymes.
In the gastrointestinal and respiratory tract, movement due to peristalsis
or cilia, respectively, helps remove infectious agents. Also, mucus traps
infectious agents. The gut flora can prevent the colonization of
pathogenic bacteria by secreting toxic substances or by competing with
2
pathogenic bacteria for nutrients or attachment to cell surfaces. Some
epithelia produce mucus which also acts as a barrier against infections. If
micro-organisms penetrate these defense systems they meet the second
line of defense including phagocytic white blood cells , antimicrobial
proteins and inflammatory response
Specific immunity (Adaptive Immunity) : immunity that an organism
develops during lifetime result of exposure to antigens(microbes, toxin or
other foreign substances) it’s the second line of defense involves
production of antibodies and generation specialized lymphocytes against
specific antigens. Specific immune response occurs in two separate

Weapon Mechanics
Players press the primary attack key to attack with their weapons, which triggers a seamless animation of the weapon's move set. The player can also use a modifier key to modify an attack in progress, depending on the Manacite socketed into the weapon. When socketed into a weapon, Manacite allows the weapon to make attacks in the Neutral Mana type and the Mana types of the Manacite socketed. Intercepting, recording, or divulging private communication—Consent required—Exceptions.
(1) Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, it shall be unlawful for any individual, partnership, corporation, association, or the state of Washington, its agencies, and political subdivisions to intercept, or record any:
(a) Private communication transmitted by telephone, telegraph, radio, or other device between two or more individuals between points within or without the state by any device electronic or otherwise designed to record and/or transmit said communication regardless how such device is powered or actuated, without first obtaining the consent of all the participants in the communication;
(b) Private conversation, by any device electronic or otherwise designed to record or transmit such conversation regardless how the device is powered or actuated without first obtaining the consent of all the persons engaged in the conversation.
(2) Notwithstanding subsection (1) of this section, wire communications or conversations (a) of an emergency nature, such as the reporting of a fire, medical emergency, crime, or disaster, or (b) which convey threats of extortion, blackmail, bodily harm, or other unlawful requests or demands, or (c) which occur anonymously or repeatedly or at an extremely inconvenient hour, or (d) which relate to communications by a hostage holder or barricaded person as defined in RCW 70.85.100, whether or not conversation ensues, may be recorded with the consent of one party to the conversation.
(3) Where consent by all parties is needed pursuant to this chapter, consent shall be considered obtained whenever one party has announced to all other parties engaged in the communication or conversation, in any reasonably effective manner, that such communication or conversation is about to be recorded or transmitted: PROVIDED, That if the conversation is to be recorded that said announcement shall also be recorded.
(4) An employee of any regularly published newspaper, magazine, wire service, radio station, or television station acting in the course of bona fide news gathering duties on a full-time or contractual or part-time basis, shall be deemed to have consent to record and divulge communications or conversations otherwise prohibited by this chapter if the consent is expressly given or if the recording or transmitting device is readily apparent or obvious to the speakers. Withdrawal of the consent after the communication has been made shall not prohibit any such employee of a newspaper, magazine, wire service, or radio or television station from divulging the communication or conversation.
(5) This section does not apply to the recording of custodial interrogations pursuant to RCW 10.122.040.

The primary driver is captured from Polestar's Order Management System (POMS). The service listens to order events from POMS. If an order event contains a valid VIN and Polestar ID in the "Driver" field, the service saves that Polestar ID as the car's primary driver. A Polestar ID is valid if it exists in the Polestar ID service (which can be confirmed with an API call). A VIN is valid if it exists in Volvo's factory order system, the Vehicle Internet Sale & Traceability Application (VISTA).

The service also stores all the events it receives in an "event store" for replay purposes. Additionally, the service allows other systems to change a car's primary driver through an API. There are two versions of the API: one with M2M authentication and one with Polestar ID authentication (OAuth). Using the Polestar ID Auth. version, the user can only edit a car's primary driver if they have access to the logged-in primary driver's credentials.

The service also saves related information for primary driver changes. This includes the system that made the update, the timestamp of when the primary driver was registered, the user ID (if the change was made using Polestar ID auth API), the client ID of the service that made the change (if the change was made using M2M auth API), and the event ID that caused the change. Originally, John defined redundant information as information that is conserved under a certain resampling process (essentially Gibbs sampling): given initial samples of variables 

\(X_1, \ldots, X_n\)

, you repeatedly pick one of the variables at random and resample it conditioned on the samples of all the other variables. The information that you still have about the original variable values after resampling many times must have been redundant, i.e. contained in at least two variables. In practice, we probably don’t want such a loose definition of redundancy: what we care about is information that is highly redundant, i.e. present in many variables. This means we would resample several variables at a time.

TLDR:

Reconstructing visual experiences from human brain activity offers a unique way to understand how the brain represents the world, and to interpret the connection between computer vision models and our visual system. While deep generative models have recently been employed for this task, reconstructing realistic images with high semantic fidelity is still a challenging problem. Here, we propose a new method based on a diffusion model (DM) to reconstruct images from human brain activity obtained via functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). More specifically, we rely on a latent diffusion model (LDM) termed Stable Diffusion. This model reduces the computational cost of DMs, while preserving their high generative performance. We also characterize the inner mechanisms of the LDM by studying how its different components (such as the latent vector Z, conditioning inputs C, and different elements of the denoising U-Net) relate to distinct brain functions. We show that our proposed method can reconstruct high-resolution images with high fidelity in straightforward fashion, without the need for any additional training and fine-tuning of complex deep-learning models. We also provide a quantitative interpretation of different LDM components from a neuroscientific perspective. Overall, our study proposes a promising method for reconstructing images from human brain activity, and provides a new framework for understanding DMs.

However, satellite data is heavily affected by weather phenomena such as the presence of clouds, haze, and snow, which limits its applicability. This drawback is partially alleviated by the recurrence of data acquisition, that increases the probability of finding pixels free from such weather effects, hence enabling the replacement of affected areas with temporally close data. Nonetheless, applying this method at scale requires to identify affected pixels accurately and automatically. To that end, we leveraged Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, and month-long Sentinel-2 time series to compose cloud-free mosaics in an automatic manner. To do so, we increased spatial resolution of all 20- and 60-meters bands of each Sentinel-2 scene in a time series to 10 meters by applying the super-resolution CNN model DSen2. The semantic segmentation CNN model HRNet was then applied on super-resolved scenes to detect pixels covered by haze, snow, and clouds, as well as their shadows, generating binary invalid pixels masks. These masks were then used to calculate pixel-wise weights of each scene in the time series according to proximity to invalid pixels and the difference between scene’s acquisition date and the central date of the month. Once weights are computed, a pixel-wise weighted average of all scenes in a time series is computed for all 12 bands, resulting in a 10m resolution cloud-free Sentinel-2 mosaic. Results show that this methodology can reliably compose cloud-free mosaics given enough scenes in the time series, while preserving pixel information of temporally close scenes and avoiding artifacts that could hamper the applicability of this method.

By Claire Cain Miller, Adam Playford, Larry Buchanan and Aaron Krolik Dec. 26, 2022

It’s hard to fully grasp the enormous potential of ChatGPT, a new artificial intelligence chatbot released last month. The bot doesn’t just search and summarize information that already exists. It creates new content, tailored to your request, often with a startling degree of nuance, humor and creativity. Most of us have never seen anything like it outside of science fiction.

To better understand what ChatGPT can do, we decided to see if people could tell the difference between the bot’s writing and a child’s.

We used real essay prompts from the National Assessment of Educational Progress (the standardized test from the Department of Education, known as the nation’s report card). We asked the bot to produce essays based on those prompts — sometimes with a little coaching, and always telling it to write like a student of the appropriate age. We put what it wrote side by side with sample answers written by real children.

We asked some experts on children’s writing to take our variation on the Turing test, live on a call with us. They were a fourth-grade teacher; a professional writing tutor; a Stanford education professor; and Judy Blume, the beloved children’s author. Background
Knicks Go is a gray horse who was bred by Angie Moore and her daughter Sabrina at GreenMount Farm in Reisterstown, Maryland. He is from the second crop of Paynter, who won the Haskell Invitational, then received widespread social media attention during his battle against a near-fatal case of colitis and laminitis. Knicks Go was produced by Kosmo's Buddy, a stakes-winning daughter of Outflanker who was claimed by the Moores for $40,000 near the end of a 37-race career.[3]

Knicks Go was sold as a weanling for $40,000 at the 2016 Keeneland November sale to Northface Bloodstock. He was resold as a yearling at the Keeneland September 2017 sale for $87,000 to the Korea Racing Authority. He was originally trained by Ben Colebrook and was transferred to the stable of Brad Cox at the end of 2019.

The colt was named for the K-nicks breeding system used by the Korea Racing Authority (KRA), with the "K" standing for Korea and nicks referring to the above average success of certain sires when bred to mares from certain other sire lines.
